canonical_statement: The study asked whether commonly used medical-consultation assistants perform first-contact interview work before giving advice and whether a short entry-to-care instruction changes that behavior.

The authors constructed four physician-authored, two- to four-turn vignettes that began with incomplete, misspelled, benignly framed patient messages and disclosed risk-relevant facts over later turns; the cases were selected demonstrations rather than a prevalence sample.

Fixed-script testing used OpenAI chat-latest, Google gemini-3.5-flash, and Anthropic claude-sonnet-4-6 on 28 July 2026 under baseline and instruction conditions, with one run per case, model, and condition, yielding 24 transcripts; the entry-to-care system prompt was the only planned condition difference.

Adaptive testing was performed for the vomiting and calf-pain cases across all three models and both conditions; a gemini-3.5-flash patient simulator answered only questions asked by the tested model, while prespecified unsafe-plan statements were inserted comparably, yielding 12 adaptive transcripts.

The entry-to-care instruction required the model to first make the concern clinically usable, then catch unsafe plans, route to an appropriate level of care without reflexive emergency escalation, and provide a concise handoff when recommending care.

canonical_statement: Transcripts were reviewed against four prespecified domains—usable concern, premise repair, safe routing, and handoff readiness—and observable markers were counted descriptively; advice before elicitation was treated as a sequencing marker rather than automatically unsafe, and no inferential statistics were reported.

The supplementary scoring rubric assigned 0, 1, or 2 points separately for usable concern, premise repair, safe routing, and handoff readiness, with explicit guidance not to interpret handoff presence as a blinded clinical-quality rating.

canonical_statement: In the baseline vomiting case, all three models initially supplied home-care or red-flag advice framed around food poisoning or dehydration; none initially asked about chronic illness or regular medications, and one asked no questions.

Baseline first-turn self-care before clot-risk questions occurred in all three calf-pain runs and in two of three upper-abdominal-pain runs, whereas all three baseline chest-pain runs began with emergency red flags and questions; the sequencing difference was greatest for benign-sounding openers.

Once the scripted patient disclosed skipped insulin or unilateral calf swelling after travel, all three models recognized possible diabetic ketoacidosis or venous thrombosis and escalated advice, indicating that relevant knowledge was often present after decisive facts were supplied.

Instruction-condition replies rejected unsafe plans earlier and more explicitly and more often separated same-day assessment from emergency criteria, but some replies still used absolute or alarmist language.

source_anchor.paragraph: Premise Repair and Routing; Handoff and Adaptive Testing

canonical_statement: The adaptive runs showed that improved sequencing did not reliably solve decisive-fact elicitation: no instruction-condition vomiting run elicited diabetes before the prespecified disclosure, even though all models escalated after the risk fact appeared.
The authors conclude that the preformulation gap should be evaluated directly through observable first-contact behavior rather than inferred from diagnostic accuracy or final-answer quality.

The authors argue that patient-facing benchmarks should begin from raw informal patient narratives and preserve misspellings, minimization, mistaken attribution, unclear timelines, and unsafe plans, while combining fixed scripts with adaptive patient simulation.

The authors recommend scoring symptom elicitation, premise repair, urgency routing, self-care safety, abstention, and handoff fidelity as separate functions because success in one does not establish success in the others.

For first-contact health assistants, the authors recommend explicit workflow specifications for minimum information elicitation, unsafe-plan interruption, same-day versus emergency thresholds, abstention, and clinician handoff; the study does not establish that such a workflow is clinically safe.

The authors state that instruction-level fixes should be treated as stopgaps requiring their own evaluation rather than substitutes for training and benchmark design targeting the preformulation stage.

This was a structured demonstration rather than a comparative clinical performance study; four English vignettes with one run per model and condition cannot estimate failure prevalence or rank vendors.
The 12 fixed-script case-model cells per condition were repeated evaluations of four vignettes across three models, not independent clinical observations.
The study included neither a human comparator nor a benign control set.

Case-specific routing expectations and transcript review were defined by the study team and were not independently blinded or externally validated, and handoff presence was not a blinded rating of handoff usefulness.

The tested API models approximate but do not reproduce consumer web products, which may add product-specific routing, safety layers, memory, or account-level controls; OpenAI chat-latest was also a moving alias rather than a fixed snapshot.
The adaptive standardized patient was itself an LLM and may differ from real patient answers.
The four-step entry-to-care instruction was not ablated, so the study cannot identify which instruction component produced the observed effects.
System-level instruction effects may change with model updates and cannot guarantee elicitation coverage.
Complete fixed-script and adaptive standardized-patient transcripts, along with code, cases, prompts, and results, are reported as publicly available in the companion repository.
